name: Black lounge suit

lead: The black lounge suit is a men's semi-formal daytime outfit: a black, midnight-blue or grey lounge jacket worn with grey striped trousers. It is known as the stroller in the US and the Stresemann in continental Europe, and it sits between formal morning dress and a conventional business suit.

It helps appearance through tailoring and dress-code fit: a well-cut dark jacket with contrasting trousers gives a long, structured line and signals polish at weddings, diplomatic or other daytime formal events. Its decline after the Second World War means it now reads as a distinctive, traditional choice.

paras: Wearers pair the jacket with striped morning trousers, a waistcoat and a restrained shirt and tie as a substitute for a morning coat. Tailoring and fabric quality are what people emphasise. It is typically reserved for daytime weddings and similar events, and some professions and fraternal bodies still use it.
No health risks. The main practical limit is that it is uncommon, so it can look out of place at events where lounge or business suits are the norm.

lead: The black lounge suit, called the stroller in the United States and the Stresemann in continental Europe, is a men's day outfit intermediate between formal morning dress and a conventional lounge suit. It combines grey striped or check morning trousers with a lounge-length jacket, single- or double-breasted, in black, midnight blue or grey [1].

For someone trying to look sharper, it offers the structured silhouette of formal tailoring in a jacket that is simpler and shorter than a morning coat. Dress-code charts list it as semi-formal, alongside black tie [2].

The outfit took its continental name from Chancellor Gustav Stresemann, who wore it during the 1925 Locarno Treaty negotiations. Its use fell after the Second World War as daytime formality declined [1].

paras: Wikipedia describes the ensemble as grey striped or check morning trousers with a conventional-length lounge jacket in black, midnight blue or grey. Early prototypes appeared in the late 19th century and the form was largely settled around 1900 [1]. Regional names include the Marlborough suit in the UK, stroller or club coat in the US, the Bonn suit in Germany and director's suit in Japan [1].

The lounge suit began in late 19th-century Britain as sportswear and country clothing, and by the early 20th century it had replaced the black frock coat as everyday daywear [2]. Around 1900 lounge suits were not usually plain black, since black was reserved for formal dress and mourning; the black lounge suit arose as a less formal alternative to white tie [2].

Stresemann wore the outfit in 1925, giving the continental name; Churchill was photographed in it in 1943 and Ronald Reagan wore one at his 1981 inauguration [1]. Declining daytime formality after the war reduced its use [1].

It is now unusual in the UK but still appears at some daytime fraternal meetings such as Freemasonry, and some barristers wear the striped trousers [1]. Its decline has been linked to the fall of morning dress and white tie, and to an old association with uniformed servants [1]. Forum discussions of formalwear for weddings treat a dark suit or tuxedo choice as dependent on the time of day and formality [3].
